papers.title: Hydrogel electrodeposition based on bipolar electrochemistry.
papers.abstract: Bipolar electrochemistry has attracted great interest for applications based on sensing, electrografting, and electrodeposition, because the technique enables electrochemical reactions to be induced at multiple bipolar electrodes (BPEs) with only a single power supply. However, there are only a few reports on the biofabrication of hydrogels using BPEs. In this study, we applied bipolar electrochemistry to achieve the electrodeposition of calcium-alginate hydrogels at specified target areas, which is possible because of the use of water electrolysis to obtain acidification at the anodic pole. This scheme was used to successfully fabricate an array of hydrogel deposits at a BPE array. In addition, hydrogels were successfully fabricated either at only the target BPEs or only the target areas of BPEs by repositioning the driving electrodes. Furthermore, a hydrogel was drawn on a large BPE as a canvas by using small driving electrodes. As a demonstration of the electrodeposited hydrogels for bioapplications, mammal cells were cultured in the hydrogels. Because the amount and shape of the hydrogel deposits can be controlled by using the bipolar system, the system we developed can be used for biosensors and cell culture platforms.

summary_en.motivation: This study aims to apply bipolar electrochemistry for the localized electrodeposition of hydrogels using a single power supply.
summary_en.method: The technique employs water electrolysis to generate localized acidification at the anodic pole, enabling calcium-alginate hydrogel formation on bipolar electrode arrays.
summary_en.result: The method successfully fabricates hydrogel arrays and patterns, and demonstrates the ability to culture mammalian cells within the deposited hydrogels.
summary_en.validation: In vitro cell culture experiments confirm the biocompatibility of the electrodeposited hydrogels.

papers.title: 3D-Printed Biosensor Arrays for Medical Diagnostics.
papers.abstract: While the technology is relatively new, low-cost 3D printing has impacted many aspects of human life. 3D printers are being used as manufacturing tools for a wide variety of devices in a spectrum of applications ranging from diagnosis to implants to external prostheses. The ease of use, availability of 3D-design software and low cost has made 3D printing an accessible manufacturing and fabrication tool in many bioanalytical research laboratories. 3D printers can print materials with varying density, optical character, strength and chemical properties that provide the user with a vast array of strategic options. In this review, we focus on applications in biomedical diagnostics and how this revolutionary technique is facilitating the development of low-cost, sensitive, and often geometrically complex tools. 3D printing in the fabrication of microfluidics, supporting equipment, and optical and electronic components of diagnostic devices is presented. Emerging diagnostics systems using 3D bioprinting as a tool to incorporate living cells or biomaterials into 3D printing is also reviewed.

summary_en.motivation: To review the application of 3D printing in fabricating biosensor arrays for low-cost medical diagnostics.
summary_en.method: The paper summarizes 3D printing techniques for microfluidics, optical, and electronic components of diagnostic devices.
summary_en.result: 3D printing enables low-cost, geometrically complex diagnostic tools, including emerging bioprinting approaches.
summary_en.validation: This is a review article without original experimental validation.
